title: Sell Mineral Rights in Worland, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Worland, WY | Washakie County
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in or around Worland, WY? We buy Bighorn Basin oil, gas, and royalty interests. Deed history checked at the Washakie County Clerk's office.
heroLead: Worland is the county seat, so if you hold a mineral interest anywhere in Washakie County, the paperwork trail almost always runs back through the clerk's office right here in town.
intro: Worland sits on the Bighorn River in the middle of Washakie County, built up around irrigated farm ground and, not far below the surface, a Bighorn Basin production history that goes back generations. The Washakie County Clerk's office here holds the deed books, probate files, and division orders for mineral interests spread across the whole county, which makes Worland the practical starting point for any title check we run.

Ownership around town tends to trace back to early 1900s homestead patents along the river bottom, with minerals split off from the surface at some point as oil activity in the basin picked up through the middle of the last century. A lot of what we see is small fractional interests, held by heirs who've long since moved away from the ranch their family proved up.

sections.heading: Production History Close to Town
paragraphs: The Tensleep Sandstone and the Phosphoria beneath it have been the workhorse zones for Bighorn Basin oil for close to a century, and Washakie County fields like Big Sand Draw and Winkleman Dome sit within reasonable range of Worland. This is mature-basin behavior - long, gradual decline curves, periodic workovers, and re-entries rather than a sudden new-well spike. A royalty check tied to a well that's been running for thirty years pays differently than one three years off its peak, and we look at the actual curve before we value anything.

sections.heading: Why the Clerk's Office Matters Here
paragraphs: Because Worland is the county seat, the recorded deed history for mineral interests all across Washakie County lives in the same building. That's useful and it's also why we don't skip it - old mineral deeds from the 1940s and 1950s sometimes carry legal descriptions or unit names that don't line up cleanly with how a tract is described on today's plat, and the only way to sort that out is by pulling the actual book and page.

sections.heading: What We Typically Buy Around Worland
paragraphs: Small fractional royalty interests inherited from a family homestead, non-producing mineral acreage that's never had a well on it, and interests complicated by an estate that never got fully settled. We buy directly from heirs, we don't require every family member to agree before we can close on one person's share, and we handle the recording at the courthouse once the deal's done.

faqs.question: Where are mineral deed records kept for property near Worland?
faqs.answer: At the Washakie County Clerk's office in Worland, since the town is the county seat. That's where our title check starts for any interest in this area.

faqs.question: Is my mineral interest tied to an active well?
faqs.answer: It depends on the tract. Washakie County has decades of Bighorn Basin production, so plenty of interests carry royalty history, but plenty of others are undeveloped acreage that's never been leased or drilled.

faqs.question: I only own a small fractional share from a family estate. Is it worth selling?
faqs.answer: Often yes, especially if you're tired of tracking annual division order statements or county tax notices for an interest you'll never develop yourself. We evaluate fractional shares individually.
